I started out with the argument that the turkish people have to learn that other countries have different customs. And they have to accept that many countries do not respect "holy" persons of their faith, since many countries are not near theocracies. I had a rather long answer to that one:

Do you know the concept of cultural relativity? It says that no aspect of a culture can be inherently better or worse than an aspect of another culture, just different. A rather logical concept, based on the idea that everything is subjective and can only be viewed in relation to each other, since there is no objective truth which can be used as a measuring tool.

But I do not agree with that view in its entirety.

I think that it isn't possible for an entire culture and all of its aspects to be inherently better or worse than another culture and all of its aspects. >But single aspects can certainly be better if they minimize grief and maximize happiness on the long-term for humanity as a whole.

Taking your Jesus analogy, for example. Europe wasn't that different in past times. If someone critcized Jesus and some aspect of the dominant church they more often than not were shunned as outcasts of society or were just killed.

But nonetheless, people fought against that and part by part created a shift in society which led to shunning or killing critics of the christian faith as being unacceptable.

This led to far less grief being created by members of the christian faith agains critics despite widespread criticism of their faith. At the same time, many people were happier because they were free express most of their views.

In nearly every islamic society it is today, like in past europe, acepptable to shun or kill critics of the dominant faith, namely Islam. Which leads to a lot of grief.

Maybe the same development could be started in islamic society, like in past europe when they are forced to be confronted with criticism of their faith and have to learn to cope with it, especially when the old coping mechanisms, violence and shunning don't work anymore.

That will lead on the short-term to grief, since many will react with violence but on the long-term it would reduce grief by a large margin.

As far as I am concerned when it comes to coping with religious criticism most western cultures are far superior in that aspect than any middle-eastern culture.

Said friend thought that was a very interesting view, which we should discuss further in the near future.

Maybe I am a bit too optimistic in my view, but what do you all think about my train of thought regarding that topic?
